BBC Wildlife (Discover Wildlife), Peregrine falcon facts: folds wings and tail into a teardrop shape and strikes prey in mid-air with its talons; the tomial tooth, a notch on the upper bill, breaks the prey's neck and spinal cord; tubercles in the nostrils slow incoming air so it can breathe while diving; a semi-transparent nictitating membrane protects the eyes at top speed; nests on high-rise blocks and cathedrals as replicas of its cliff ledges; feral pigeons are common urban prey; https://www.discoverwildlife.com/animal-facts/birds/peregrine-falcon-facts

beats.say: This bird hits its prey at two hundred miles an hour. Feet first.
The peregrine falcon. The fastest bird in the world.
It climbs more than half a mile into the sky.
Then it folds its wings into a teardrop, and drops.
It punches a bird right out of the air, with its talons.
At that speed, how does it even breathe? Tiny bumps in its nostrils slow the rushing air.
And a see-through third eyelid slides over each eye, like built in goggles.
Fifty years ago, it almost vanished. The bug spray DDT poisoned it.
Its eggshells got so thin, they cracked under the parents.
By nineteen seventy five, North America was down to three hundred twenty four pairs.
Then it came back. And it moved to the city.
Skyscrapers are its new cliffs. Pigeons are its new snack.
If a pigeon survives the hit, a notch on its beak finishes the job. It bites through the neck.
Would you want one nesting on your building?
Two hundred miles an hour, just to eat the pigeons off your window.
Follow me. Next, a frog whose heart stops all winter.
